evidence.title: Assessing the Impact of the Quality of Textual Data on Feature Representation and Machine Learning Models: Quantitative Study Using Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Predictive performance by dataset error rate
evidence.effect: Errors at <10% were tolerated; ROC-AUC performance significantly deteriorated at ≥10%.
evidence.quote: By comparing the performance of models on datasets with varying error rates (evaluated in terms of ROC-AUC), we observed that models were relatively tolerant to smaller error rates (<10%) but their performance significantly deteriorated at higher error rates (≥10%).

commentary.bottom_line: Twelve sources endorse data management plans, standardized preparation, and recurring data-quality checks for each AI solution, but no study has tested whether these practices improve AI performance or protect personal data. One offline benchmark suggests that model discrimination holds up at data error rates below 10% and declines at 10% or higher, which shows the hazard exists without testing the safeguard.

perspectives.view: No study tests the recommended practice, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single hazard study is a level 5 automated benchmark in an offline setting with 42,110 older-adult patients. It reports that ROC-AUC deteriorated at error rates of 10% or more, which is indirect evidence about data quality and says nothing about management plans.

The benchmark suggests a possible threshold: errors below 10% were tolerated, and performance dropped at 10% or higher. If that pattern holds in live settings, recurring quality evaluation might catch degradation before it affects predictions. No study shows that such evaluation detects errors in time or prevents harm, and the privacy exposure named in the hazard was not examined.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software lists explicit term definitions as a may-level practice and gives the example of a sex field that one party codes as sex at birth and another as self-reported. NIST AI 600-1 asks organizations to document data accuracy and representativeness across the life cycle. Both documents rest on expert consensus rather than on trial data.

The only study drew on older adults in the United States and Australia and did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. Data errors and missing fields may cluster in records for these patients, so an overall error-rate threshold could hide higher error rates in subgroups. No evidence addresses this question.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares AI performance, data-quality drift, or privacy incidents between deployments with and without a documented data management plan, standardized preprocessing, or scheduled quality audits. Prospective evaluations in live clinical settings should measure how often recurring checks detect errors near the 10% level reported in the benchmark, what the checks cost in staff time, and whether they reduce downstream harm or data exposure.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, and the one hazard study included older adults without reporting Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no evidence on whether data-quality procedures perform equally well for their patients or whether error rates in their records exceed the tolerated range.
